sections.h2: What does the Orange County Official Records system hold?
sections.html:
The Orange County Comptroller's Official Records Department records, indexes and archives the documents that make up the county's Official Records. Its own description lists deeds, mortgages, satisfactions, claims of lien, final judgments and orders, notices of commencement and declarations of domicile.

For a seller in Orange County, this is the place where the paper trail on a house lives. A buyer's title agent will search it for every mortgage, lien and judgment tied to your name or your parcel before closing. Reading the same index yourself, before you list, shows what that agent is going to find.

  • Deeds and mortgages that show who owns the parcel and who lent against it
  • Satisfactions that show a loan was paid off and released
  • Claims of lien, which can come from contractors or associations and must be cleared before a clean sale
  • Final judgments recorded against an owner
  • Notices of commencement, which signal recent construction work

sections.h2: Who keeps which Orange County records?
sections.html:
Recorded land documents sit with the Orange County Comptroller, while a different office runs the circuit and county court case files. In Florida the clerk of the circuit court is the officer who records documents and collects documentary stamp tax at recording, and in Orange County the Comptroller's Official Records Department carries out that recording work.

The Property Appraiser is a third office. It keeps the ownership, value and exemption record for each parcel, and its home page offers property search, a tax estimator, forms and tax roll information. The Tax Collector bills and collects the tax. If a question is about a recorded deed or lien, start with the Comptroller. If it is about assessed value or a homestead exemption, start with the Property Appraiser.

sections.h2: How do I search Orange County property records before selling?
sections.html:
Use the Official Records page on the Comptroller's website at occompt.com, then run the index search by owner name or by the legal description of the parcel. Search every name that has ever been on the deed, including a spouse or a trust, because a lien recorded against a former owner can still sit on the chain of title.

Pair that search with the Property Appraiser's parcel record so that the legal description, owner of record and homestead status all agree. A mismatch between a mailing address, a surname or a legal description is easier to fix before you have a buyer waiting. If a recorded item looks wrong or unfamiliar, ask the Comptroller's Official Records Department how to get a certified copy, and ask a title company or a Florida attorney what it means for your sale.

The Official Records index is a finding aid. Treat a search screen as a lead to the recorded instrument, and get a certified copy from the Comptroller when a lender, court or title agent needs a formal one.

sections.h2: What will a deed filing in Orange County run me?
sections.html:
A filing adds up from page charges plus documentary stamp tax, and the stamp tax usually outweighs the page charges. State law sets the deed rate at 70 cents on each $100 of consideration, and the Department of Revenue says Miami-Dade is the only county on a different schedule, so Orange County follows the standard rate.

The Department of Revenue also states that all parties to the document are liable for the tax whichever party agrees to pay it, and that it is gathered at the recording counter. Consideration counts money, the discharge of an obligation and any mortgage or encumbrance, whether or not the buyer assumes it.

Charges that can apply to a recorded deed (state statutes and Florida Department of Revenue)

Clerk page charge, first page$5.00 (s. 28.24)
Clerk page charge, each added page$4.00 (s. 28.24)

Before you mail or submit a deed, ask the Comptroller's Official Records Department for the current total, since page count and the number of names change the bill.

sections.h2: Can I record electronically in Orange County?
sections.html:
Yes. The Comptroller's Official Records Department accepts eRecording through approved vendors, and its page lists Record Nation, Deeds and eRecording USA in alphabetical order without recommending any of them.

You scan the document and upload it through the vendor's application. The original never leaves your hands, and funds for transfer taxes, recording fees and a small vendor fee move by ACH. The page says documents are typically recorded the same day when submitted during regular business hours, and that you can retrieve the stamped image right after recording. For questions, the department lists 407-836-5111 for eRecording.

  • Title companies and attorneys usually handle this step at closing
  • A private seller can use a vendor, but the deed still needs proper signatures, witnesses and a legal description
  • Keep the recorded image with your closing file

sections.h2: What happens to a deed on tax certificate or tax deed property?
sections.html:
If taxes stay unpaid, the Tax Collector sells a tax certificate, and a certificate left unredeemed for two years can lead to a tax deed application. The Tax Collector's site says tax deed sales in Orange County are processed through the Comptroller's Office, and the Comptroller's page confirms that tax deed auctions are performed by the Official Records Department.

State statute says the clerk holds the public auction, that the high bidder posts a nonrefundable deposit of 5 percent of the bid or $200, whichever is greater, and that the rest of the money plus recording charges is due within 24 hours, excluding weekends and holidays. A homeowner who is behind on taxes should pay the Tax Collector before this stage. The tax office pages explain how to redeem a certificate, and a tax deed payoff is a separate figure from an ordinary current-year bill.

sections.h2: What does the Orange County recording picture look like?
sections.html:
Orange County is the most populous county in Central Florida, and recording volume follows its size. QuickFacts shows 1,528,002 residents as of July 1, 2025, a 6.9 percent gain over the 2020 base, with 614,386 housing units and 13,140 building permits issued during 2025.

Just over 56 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, and the five-year survey puts the middle home value at $390,100. All of this sits on 902.02 square miles of land. That mix of owners, renters and new construction explains why searches here often turn up notices of commencement, association liens and several mortgages on one chain of title.

sections.h2: How can an Orange County seller use the records to sell faster?
sections.html:
Pull your own records first, then clear what you can. A recorded mortgage with no matching satisfaction, an old contractor claim or an unreleased judgment can each stall a closing for weeks.

  • Search the index under every owner name and any prior spelling
  • Confirm each paid-off loan shows a recorded satisfaction
  • Ask the Property Appraiser to correct a wrong mailing address or exemption record
  • Check with the Tax Collector that no current or past taxes are open
  • Hand your title agent the list so surprises surface early

If the title is messy or you need to sell quickly as is, a direct cash buyer can often work around these items. Compare any offer with the lien payoff figures in your own records.

faqs.q: Where do I search Orange County deeds and mortgages?
faqs.a: Use the Orange County Comptroller's Official Records Department. Its page at occompt.com explains the department and links to the record search. Deeds, mortgages, satisfactions and liens are all recorded there.

faqs.q: Who pays documentary stamp tax on a deed in Orange County?
faqs.a: The Department of Revenue says all parties to the document are liable no matter who agrees to pay. In a sale the seller commonly pays by contract, but the contract decides it. The clerk collects the tax at recording, at 70 cents per $100 of consideration.

faqs.q: Is Orange County's Official Records the same as court records?
faqs.a: No. The Comptroller's Official Records Department keeps recorded instruments such as deeds, liens and recorded judgments. Court case files are kept by the clerk of the courts. Ask the right office for the right record.

faqs.q: Can I record a deed online in Orange County?
faqs.a: Yes, through the approved eRecording vendors the Comptroller lists. You upload a scan, pay taxes and fees by ACH, and documents are typically recorded the same day when sent during regular business hours. The department lists 407-836-5111 for eRecording questions.

faqs.q: Do unpaid property taxes affect recording a sale in Orange County?
faqs.a: They affect closing more than recording. Taxes are due by March 31 and turn delinquent on April 1, and a certificate sale follows on or before June 1. Ask the Orange County Tax Collector for a payoff figure so the title agent can clear it at closing.
